skill-create-skill.title: kes-create-skill: create, edit and review skills the right way
skill-create-skill.note: Interviews you into a 7-part brief, builds the skill at level L1/L2/L3, runs an independent review and a 20-prompt trigger test. Version 1.1.0, by KesFlow - Hưng Kescy.

sections.t: Use it when you want to create, write, edit, compress or review a Claude Code skill, or when a skill won't trigger. Triggered by: create skill, write skill, edit skill, update skill, review skill, compress skill, optimize skill, make this a skill.
Goal: predictable behavior

AI agents are random: ask the same question twice and you may get different answers. A skill doesn't force the same result, it forces the same process every time. The wording can change, the method can't. Every technique in this kit serves that goal.
Not for: running a skill you already installed, writing SOPs or docs for human readers, or building automated workflows.
Three branches at run time

head: You say
Branch
Path
rows: Interview, brief, lock the level, build from template, review, trigger test, trial run, package 1.0.0
Read the whole original, save a snapshot, lock the intent, edit, review with a claims ledger, bump the version
Review this skill, don't change it
An independent reviewer scores against the checklist and only reports findings

sections.t: The Create branch step by step

items.d: Ask in clusters of 3 to 5 questions, each with a suggested answer. There are 5 anti-overfit questions: what changes between runs, 3 nearby cases to handle, 3 look-alike prompts that must not trigger, who else will use it and how they phrase it, what event would make the skill outdated.
A fresh reviewer reads the brief and keeps asking until it returns NO GAPS. Then you must explicitly approve.
L1 tool guide, L2 workflow, L3 router. Decide before building.
Present the file tree and structure; once approved, build from the templates in assets.
Every finding must be answered: fixed, or disagreed with a reason.
Check that the description triggers when it should and stays quiet when it should.
One clean run, tag version 1.0.0 and a dated changelog.

sections.t: How to interview for a brief
Goal: turn a vague 'make me a skill' into a brief good enough for a stranger to build the skill without asking again, and general enough not to be stuck on the one case you just ran.

items: Ask in small groups of 3 to 5 related questions per turn, each with why it's asked plus Claude's suggested answer and reasoning, because fixing a wrong guess is faster than filling a blank.
Read first, ask later: read the conversation, files and existing skills. If you say 'turn what we just did into a skill', extract from that run first.
When you give both source docs and instructions (e.g. 'here are the docs, focus on auth and pagination'), the instructions are hard requirements, not commentary.
Unlike a problem brief, a skill brief may state triggers, level, outputs and steps.
Stop when it can predict your next 3 answers (about 95%), then draft the brief.
You must clearly approve the brief; 'up to you' or silence doesn't count. After edits, confirm again.

sections.t: 5 anti-overfit questions (all 5 required)
The default failure is overfitting: you describe the exact case you just did, and the skill only triggers on that case.

head: Question
What it reveals
rows: Name 3 situations the skill should handle even if you haven't hit them yet
Name 3 prompts that look similar but must NOT trigger the skill
The must-stay-quiet half of the trigger test
Who else will use it, and how do they phrase things differently from you?
What event would make the skill wrong, and what signal says it needs updating?

sections.t: Answers about near-misses and about what makes the skill outdated are recorded verbatim for the trigger test and the update conditions.
Brief review by an independent reviewer

A subagent with no context from the interview cold-reads the brief with one instruction: build the skill from the brief without asking the requester, checking two angles: is it complete, and is it stuck on a single case. Each gap becomes a question; Claude asks you, updates the brief, and re-checks until it returns exactly NO GAPS.
The brief has 7 parts (fixed order)

head: Part
Content
rows: What the skill lets the agent do (1 line) and where it stops (1 line)
L1, L2 or L3 with a reason; model-invoked or user-invoked, with a reason
At least 3 phrasings that must trigger and 3 look-alikes that must stay quiet
What changes between runs; branches needed every time go in SKILL.md, rare branches go to references
What the skill takes, what it produces, what a checkable 'done' looks like; if it outputs a document, lock the required structure and write it in the user's language
Things that never change across runs or edits: safety rules, data contracts, customer-facing strings
At least 3 things it deliberately doesn't do, in the form 'Doesn't do X because Y'

sections.t: The brief is written entirely in the user's language, headings included. The part numbers are a contract; don't reorder them.
Three skill levels

head: Level
What it is
Pick when
Default invocation
Lines (target / max)
rows: Teaches the agent to use one tool or API correctly; mostly reference, few or no steps
The job is using one tool correctly, not running a multi-step task
Steps for one job end to end, with a checkable output and a review gate
One job run start to finish with a checkable result; most skills live here
User-invoked if it has side effects or is time-sensitive, otherwise model-invoked
Entry point for an area: just a routing table and shared rules, does no work itself
2 or more sibling skills in one area that need a shared entry point

sections.t: Level measures one thing only: how many jobs a skill coordinates. It doesn't decide how docs are split or how the skill is invoked. Lock the level in the brief, since it sets the template, checklist and done criteria for the skill's whole life.
The frame for each level

head: Level
Content frame
Main done criteria
rows: Tool scope in one line; a table of main operations with parameter formats; common mistakes as wrong vs. right; post-action check rules; drift warning (the real tool beats the skill); destructive operations never run on their own. Add a Setup section if the tool needs login; secrets never live in the skill.

Every operation and parameter must exist in the tool's real docs; every common mistake has a wrong/right pair; state which event forces a skill update; an embedded mini workflow is about 5 steps max, longer ones become an L2.

Short intro (optional); required inputs; steps, each with a checkable done criterion; an independent review gate when the output matters; outputs with a Done-when line. If the output is a document, use a template from assets.

The Inputs section always comes first and says how to ask when something is missing; every step has a done criterion; every step that can fail names a way out (conditional retry, fallback, or stop and ask); creating a document without a template in assets fails; fixed command sequences are not written as prose.

A one-paragraph map of the area; at most 5 hard rules, each blocking one type of error; a routing table 'want X, use skill Y' including seemingly small intents, plus look-alike intents that belong elsewhere; a change policy.
Every sibling skill is in the table; every routing target exists; no executable content in the body; adding, renaming, removing or rescoping a skill updates the table in the same batch.

sections.t: For an L2 with many branches: small branches get one line in a step, big branches get their own reference file per variant, bigger still means a separate skill. With 2 or more decision points, draw a mermaid diagram showing only the flow shape above the Steps section. The skill's output speaks the user's language from start to finish.
System rules

items: One-way dependencies: L3 points to L2, L2 points to L1, a lower level never points up.
Only write commands, parameters, flags or field names when they appear verbatim in the source docs or were actually run while drafting. Plausible guesses are the top cause of broken tool guides.

The skill body is written in concise English. Vietnamese strings are kept only when a machine matches that exact string, customers read or hear it, it's an example teaching writing in that language, or it's a phrase users type to trigger the skill.

Use simple words a newcomer already knows. Jargon stays only if the skill defines it and reuses it as a leading word; jargon the reader has to look up and that isn't defined in the file is a review failure.
Naming: L1 is the tool's noun, L2 is a verb-first phrase (write plan-content, not content-planning), L3 is the area's noun.
Author: every skill has metadata.author in the form 'your name · built with kes-create-skill · KesFlow', unless you choose a different author line.
A skill of pure knowledge (theory, standards) isn't a level; it's reference material every level can cite.

sections.t: Vendor skills

Skills published by a tool vendor are read-only; update them by importing the new version, never edit in place. Put your customizations where they're just enough: a few rules go in CLAUDE.md, more than that becomes a small companion skill holding only the differences and triggered by the same keywords. Don't copy vendor content into the companion skill, it will drift when the original updates. On conflict: the companion skill beats the vendor skill, the real tool beats both.
Versioning

head: Type of change
Bump
Example
rows: A fix that doesn't change steps, branches or contracts
Add a step, branch, doc, template or trigger phrase
A change that breaks the old usage
Rename, remove or rework a step, change the output format, restructure

sections.t: Each release bumps once at the highest level touched, with a dated changelog line right below the frontmatter, in the form X.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD) — what changed. The first version is 1.0.0.
When to split a skill

items: Split one L2 into several L2s plus an L3 when 2 or more separate trigger clusters appear, or the body exceeds the line cap even with docs split properly.
An L1 embeds a mini workflow of about 5 steps max; longer than that, it becomes an L2.

sections.t: Description: where a skill lives or dies

items: Put the trigger phrases users actually type (Vietnamese included) first.
A short description of 1 to 2 sentences.
Add 1 to 2 do-not-trigger clauses for the most easily confused skill.
Max 1024 characters, no angle brackets.

sections.t: Trimming words

items: No-op test: delete any sentence that doesn't change behavior from the model's default.
Leading word: one word the model already knows can replace three sentences of explanation.
Each idea lives in one place only. When compressing an existing skill, keep a claims ledger: every idea must remain or have a reason for being cut.

sections.t: Standard vocabulary for this kit

head: Concept
Meaning
rows: The agent follows the same process every run, not the same output. A brainstorm skill still gives new ideas each time, but the way it leads is consistent.
Keep the description so the agent can trigger on its own, but the description is always in context every turn (costs context).
Drop the description and trigger only when you type the name (disable-model-invocation: true). Costs no context but you have to remember the skill exists; use it where human judgment is needed.

Move docs that rare branches need into separate files behind a pointer; what every run needs stays in SKILL.md. If a pointer fires unevenly, fix the pointer's wording first, and pull it inline only if rewording fails.
Things that must be read together sit together (definitions, rules, caveats under one heading).
The condition that tells the agent a step is done. Strongest when it's both checkable and demanding enough. Fuzzy criteria like 'understood' tend to cause early stops.
A word the model has already learned that carries a whole behavior principle (e.g. tracer bullets, tight, relentless). A word too weak to beat the default is itself a no-op; use a stronger one.
A sentence that doesn't change behavior from the model's default. If a sentence fails, delete the whole sentence, don't shave a few words.
Old text that piles up because adding feels safe and deleting feels risky. The default fate of a skill without pruning discipline.
A skill that's simply too long. Fix it with layered docs and splitting by branch.

sections.t: Three kinds of human approval gates
When a skill writes to something humans own (customer data, outgoing messages), a human is the gate. Pick the type by who creates the value, not by the number of items.

head: Type
Value comes from
Human does
Use when
rows: Each item needs a different decision
Answers the whole cluster, then hears the parsed list read back before writing
Reviews the table; silence means yes; only flags wrong rows
A deterministic signal produces the answer

sections.t: The third type is only for exact inference, not estimation (matching on values the user entered, not similarity scores). Making a reviewer check guesses is worse than asking directly. Always show both the matched part and the rest; the rest falls back to asking item by item.
Review before use

The review process covers a manual check, independent review, a claims ledger (when compressing or restructuring), trigger test and trial run. A builder grading their own work is pointless because the build context blinds them.

head: Role
Who
Does what
rows: Presents the direction (goal, scope, approach) first, edits directly only after approval, reports results honestly with a score
A fresh agent with no build context
Scores against the level's checklist in an adversarial stance: find why the skill breaks. Every comment cites file and line
Holds the direction gate at the start, doesn't approve every small change, receives the report and final score

sections.t: 1. Manual check (every round)

items: Structure: SKILL.md at the root, a flat references folder, assets, plus scripts only if the skill ships runnable scripts; no nested folders, no stray files.
Line budget within the level's cap.
Frontmatter: name matches the folder name; description follows the formula, max 1024 characters, no angle brackets; has metadata.version, metadata.author and a dated changelog.
Nothing that goes stale in the body (dates, 'currently', numbers that change).
Every referenced file exists; with 2 or more reference files, include a read-when table.

sections.t: 2. Independent review

items.d: Scores against the level's checklist and runs the no-op test on every line. Every conclusion must cite file and line; a lumped 'N out of M passed' is invalid. Missing a required core part (Inputs, Steps, Done-when for L2) means restructuring, not patching.
Fixed, or disagreed with a reason. Ignoring is not allowed.

items.t: Whoever found the issue checks the fix
items.d: Cheapest, since they already have the context.

items.t: Max 3 rounds with the same reviewer
items.d: For round 4 or after a big rewrite, use a fresh reviewer, because a reviewer who has ruled 3 times will defend old rulings. Stuck after 3 rounds: stop and hand the table of unresolved findings to the decision-maker, don't force a pass.

items.t: Fixing one error pattern means finding every variant
items.d: The locations listed in a finding are just samples. Search all of SKILL.md, references and assets before fixing, or the 'fixed' label is a lie.

sections.t: 3. Claims ledger (only when compressing or restructuring)

A fresh agent compares against the original: list every claim (rule, step, constraint, fact) and mark it kept (where it lives now) or cut with a reason. Dropping a claim without declaring it fails the edit. Then recheck the line budget, because losing claims to hit the budget is a failure.
4. Trigger test
The description is the only pointer always loaded, so a perfect skill body behind a weak description never gets reached. Run this whenever you write or change the description.

head: Group
Count
Content
rows: One intent, many phrasings: formal, casual, lowercase, typos, in the language the user types. Include a prompt that doesn't name the skill but clearly needs it, a rare case, and a case where the skill must beat a look-alike skill
Only look-alikes, taken from the near-miss questions in the interview. Each shares keywords or concepts but needs a different tool. Completely unrelated prompts are banned because they test nothing

items.d: You approve them, because bad prompts produce a bad description. Prompts must be specific: file names, real situations, one line of context.
Play the agent choosing a skill, without looking at the skill body. Record trigger or quiet.
At least 9 of 10 must-trigger prompts actually trigger AND at least 9 of 10 must-stay-quiet prompts actually stay quiet. Below the bar on either side: fix and rerun the whole set.

sections.t: When it fails: a miss means the description lacks that family of phrasings, so add it; a false trigger means a soft boundary, so state what the skill isn't for or point to the tool that owns that case.
5. Trial run

Run the full skill once on a sample request; the skill's own Done-when must hold. A skill that has never run once is just a draft. If it fails, go back to the Builder; if it passes, report results with a score using the scoring report template.
Definition of done for the whole process

items: Direction presented and approved BEFORE editing, results reported honestly afterward.
Complete brief, NO GAPS, explicit approval from you (Create branch).
Manual checks all clean.
The level checklist passes 100% with cited evidence; every line passes the no-op test and the simple-words test; a skill that creates documents has a template in assets.
Trigger test passes at least 9 of 10 on both sides.
One real trial run, Done-when holds.
Clean claims ledger (only when compressing an old skill).

sections.t: Scoring report template

The report is written in the reader's language, with these parts: a Checks table (direction, brief, static, level checklist, trigger test, trial run; items not run are marked SKIPPED with a reason, rows never deleted), a Findings table (each row has file:line, blocking or should-fix, the issue quoted verbatim, the Builder's answer), Claims ledger, Verdict (score and result) and Next steps.
What you get from using the skill

The results below are the outputs the skill itself specifies (per SKILL.md and README), not numbers measured on real projects. When you use it and get real results, note them so they can be added here.

items: A properly structured skill: SKILL.md, references, assets, version and changelog.
A 7-part brief as the basis, not stuck on a single case.
A description that passed the trigger test, so it fires at the right time and rarely misfires.
A scoring report from the template, with evidence for every finding.
Old skills compressed while keeping every idea, thanks to the claims ledger.

guide-ai-agent-theory.title: What is an AI Agent? What it really is and how it differs from an AI chatbot
guide-ai-agent-theory.note: Understand what an agent really is, how it differs from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini in Q&A mode, and what parts it's made of.

next.label: Read next: The AI Agent ecosystem (OpenClaw, Hermes, MCP…)

sections.t: One line to remember: a chatbot answers questions. An agent takes a goal, breaks it into steps, uses tools to do the work and reports back.
What an AI Agent really is

An AI Agent is a system that uses a large language model (LLM) as its “brain”, surrounded by the things that let it act: tools, memory, workflows and permissions. Instead of stopping at one answer, an agent runs in a loop until the job is done, or stops to ask you when a decision is needed.

items.d: You hand over a job, no need to give every small command.
The agent breaks the job into steps.
Search the web, read files, call APIs, run commands, control apps.
Read back what the tools return and check it matches the intent.
Keep going or change direction until the goal is reached.
Send the results, check back at important or irreversible steps.

sections.t: How an AI chatbot and an AI Agent differ

ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini… used in a Q&A chat window are AI chatbots. The same model can act as an agent when given tools, memory and permission to act. So the difference lies in how the system is built around the model, not just in the model itself.

head: Criteria
AI chatbot (Q&A)
AI Agent
rows: Complete a multi-step task (read meeting notes, create tasks, schedule…)
One turn: you ask, it answers
A loop: plan, act, check, continue
Call APIs, browse the web, read/write files, run code, control apps
Lasting across days: notes, document stores, logs
Can run on a schedule or on events, then report to you
Takes real actions itself (sends email, writes records, edits files) within granted scope
Low: if it's wrong, you see it right away
Higher: mistakes can have real consequences; needs permissions and approval
You need to be good at
Delegating clearly, setting boundaries, checking results

sections.t: The line is blurring: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini all have agent modes (tools, web browsing, running code…). Ask yourself three questions: (1) Does it plan multiple steps on its own? (2) Does it use tools to act on the outside world? (3) Does it remember and keep running when you're not there? The more “yes” answers, the more it's an agent.
A quick comparison

items.d: You paste meeting notes into the chat and ask for a summary. It returns a summary; you create the tasks and schedule yourself.
You send the notes file. The agent reads it, pulls out the action items, creates tasks, puts them on the calendar, messages the people involved and reports back to you.

sections.t: The 6 parts of an AI Agent

items.d: The language model reads intent, breaks down the work, decides the next step.
APIs, browser, files, commands, apps. The MCP standard makes connecting tools easier.
Your context and data: notes, documents, history, so you don't have to explain again.
Workflows you've packaged as instructions so the agent redoes them the right way.
Software that holds the loop, permissions, schedules, cost limits and logs.
Where you hand over work and get results: Zalo, Telegram, Slack, email…

sections.t: Levels of autonomy

items.d: You design the steps up front; AI handles a few of them (summarizing, classifying). Easiest to control.
The agent plans and acts on its own; you approve the important steps.
Runs long, decides many steps on its own; you only see results and alerts. Needs tight permissions and monitoring.

sections.t: Beginners should start at levels 1 and 2, then widen permissions gradually as they come to trust the results.
Risks to know before letting an agent work

items: Permissions too broad: the more an agent can do, the more harm a mistake causes. Grant minimum permissions.
Malicious instructions hidden in content the agent reads (emails, web pages, files), also called prompt injection. Don't let the agent follow everything it reads.
Unexpected costs: loops that run forever or call the model too often. Set a budget limit.
Mistakes nobody notices: keep logs so you can review what the agent did.
Leaked keys and data: don't put real passwords or API keys where the agent or others can read them.

sections.t: Golden rules: minimum permissions, approve every irreversible action, set a cost cap, turn on logging, keep secret keys separate from the data the agent reads.

Core principle: describe the direction in words first, lock the numbers by eye later. The skill never asks students for hex codes, fonts or corner radius; it records the feel, builds a specimen, then locks tokens from the chosen version. How it runs, step by step

items.d: The skill checks whether the root folder already has PRODUCT.md or DESIGN.md. If you mention a website or logo, it reads the quick-start section of the reference docs to shorten the visual questions.

Interviews one cluster at a time, each question with a suggested answer and a reason. Done when every section is filled or marked N/A with a reason, there is at least one real answer from the student, and you confirm the DRAFT.
Builds design-explore.html with 3 style families to choose from by eye. Every color pair must pass contrast before you see it. After you choose, tokens are locked from the chosen version.
Creates UPLOAD.md, listing which files go to Claude Design and which stay local. You can rerun the skill any time to refresh.
An independent subagent that never saw the interview checks the files against the completion criteria. Every finding must be fixed or explained.

sections.t: Phase 1: PRODUCT.md interview questions

Interviews in Vietnamese, one cluster of questions at a time, waiting for answers before the next cluster. No dumping every question at once, no trickling single isolated questions either. Each question comes with a suggested answer and a reason, because fixing a wrong guess is faster than filling a blank.

head: Cluster
Questions
rows: Product or project name (if none yet, suggest 2 to 3 working names). A one-line tagline: what it is, who it's for. 1 to 2 sentences on what the product does and what problem it solves. Register: brand (the design is the product, like a landing page, portfolio or campaign, strong expression allowed) or product (the design serves the product, like a dashboard or app, prioritizing clarity, efficiency, consistency).
Who uses it: describe a real person with a role and context, not something generic. What they need to get done when they open the product. What success looks like: one concrete sign, not 'satisfied'.

3 words for the brand's personality, avoiding 'beautiful' or 'professional' because they're too generic. 2 to 3 products or sites whose feel you want, and why each. What it must never look like (specific names). Special accessibility needs, WCAG AA by default, such as older users, large text, color blindness, reduced motion.

items: Register holds a single value, brand or product, no prose. This value also decides the sample screen set in phase 2.
Cluster 2: the skill proposes a reasonable answer based on cluster 1 as a hypothesis for the student to correct.
The must-never-look-like items (anti-references) matter a lot, because they appear word for word in the Don'ts section of DESIGN.md.
Where the wording matters, quote the student's exact words in double quotes.
No talk of colors, fonts or corner radius in this phase; that's phase 2's job.

sections.t: Deriving design principles

The skill doesn't ask directly; it derives 3 to 5 strategic principles from the answers, for example 'reading speed matters more than effects' for a product used by busy professionals. These are strategy, not visual rules (no hex codes or fonts). The skill states them for the student to confirm.
Information gate and fallback paths

items: Before writing: every section of the template is filled or marked N/A with a reason. If something is missing, go back to that cluster and ask again, never make it up. Then create PRODUCT.md in the root folder from the template, labelled [DRAFT] until the student confirms.
At least one real answer from the student is required, not synthesized from the brief.
Student only gives adjectives for personality: ask once 'if the brand were a person you met, how would they talk and dress?', then write [needs input] and move on.
No must-never-look-like items: ask once more 'what kind of design would feel wrong for this brand?'. Still nothing, write N/A and note that the Don'ts section will be derived from the principles.
File already exists: ask which file to refresh, never overwrite without asking.

The skill asks whether there's a website or page you want to follow or learn from, then classifies it. If it's your own brand, keep its identity; if it's a page you admire, take only the direction, since it isn't your brand. If there's none, run the full interview.

items: For any link, send it to context.dev's design-md-generator tool (context.dev/free-tools/design-md-generator), which returns a DESIGN.md for that page. No need to save HTML or take screenshots.

That output is only reference material, not the final file. Take the hex codes, fonts, corner radius and spacing as a draft for the DESIGN.md frontmatter, note what's missing or renamed, then still go through the pick-by-eye and contrast-check steps.
If the tool or link has changed, trust the current tool and tell the student.

Asset handling
rows: Collect the real logo and font files, and still check the fonts support Vietnamese. These assets go under Step 1 of UPLOAD.md
Don't copy the original logo or fonts: they're intellectual property and not your brand. Inherit only the style and structure. If you don't have a logo yet, note it in UPLOAD.md

sections.t: Inherited colors are not exempt from the contrast check either.
Phase 2 in detail: from feel to DESIGN.md
Phase 2 requires PRODUCT.md. Principle: describe the direction in words first, lock the numbers by eye later. Never ask students for hex codes, fonts or corner radius.

items.d: One cluster, each question with a suggested answer. (1) Core feeling: what a stranger should feel in the first 3 seconds, 3 words, the more specific the better. (2) Metaphor: if the brand were a room you walk into, what room is it, the light, the atmosphere, the materials. (3) Color personality: pick a level (a) neutrals plus one accent at no more than 10%, (b) one dominant color at 30 to 60%, (c) a 3 to 4 color palette, (d) color across the whole surface, then describe the range in words. (4) Type feel: (a) elegant serif plus friendly sans, (b) one clean sans, (c) strong display plus mono, (d) magazine style. (5) Motion energy: restrained, responsive, or choreographed. (6) Depth: flat, lightly layered or clearly raised; product should be flat or layered, brand is free. (7) Reconfirm the must-never-look-like items from PRODUCT.md.

Three families that truly differ in visual language (frame style, corner radius, depth, density, decoration, layout school), not recolors of one design. A stays closest to the student's words, B pushes the personality, C is light and easy to read (also a test: if C wins, A and B went too far). At least one family breaks away from the obvious choice. Based on styles.csv, colors.csv and a Vietnamese-ready font pair from typography.csv.

Fill specimen.html into design-explore.html in the root folder, one file with 3 tabs A, B, C. Each tab uses the brand's real copy (name, tagline, 2 to 3 sentences verbatim from PRODUCT.md, no lorem), a Vietnamese diacritics test line, the screen set for the Register, a primary button in 3 states and an embedded JS WCAG contrast reader.

items.t: Step 4: check contrast before the student looks
items.d: Every text and background pair must pass WCAG AA. If one fails, adjust the token (darker or lighter) within the family's personality; if it still fails, switch to the nearest palette in colors.csv that covers all roles. Repeat until everything passes. The student never sees a failing option.

Ask by feel: which one looks most like you. Students can mix (A's colors with B's type), applied directly to CSS variables and rechecked for contrast, with a reminder to press Ctrl+F5 and a log of every change. Reconfirm in plain words, for example 'soft, warm, rounded'.

items.t: Step 6: lock DESIGN.md from the chosen version
items.d: Read each CSS value from the confirmed version, never write from memory, because any value not in DESIGN.md gets lost downstream (Claude Design reads DESIGN.md, not the specimen). Every must-never-look-like item from PRODUCT.md goes into Don'ts verbatim. The Motion section carries the NON-SPEC EXTENSION mark.

head: Register
Sample screen set
rows: Hero, call-to-action button (3 states), proof card, short form
App shell (top or side navigation), data table row, card, form, button (3 states)

items: Student can't choose or feels they're all wrong: ask in words what's wrong, adjust the closest family and show it again, never invent a fourth family.
Chosen font fails the Vietnamese filter: replace it using vn-fonts.md, keeping the personality.
Design mode without PRODUCT.md: stop and run phase 1 first, because the Register and the must-never-look-like items are required inputs.

Mapping Vietnamese words to search keywords in the data: sang trọng is luxury or elegant, ấm áp is warm or humanist, gọn hiện đại is minimal or modern, mạnh gắt is bold or brutalist, vui is playful or rounded.

sections.t: DESIGN.md format (Stitch standard, 9 sections)

The source standard is the open-source Stitch spec (google-labs-code/design.md, 8 sections plus a version field). The skill adds a single extension, Motion, clearly marked as non-standard. The frontmatter is mandatory and machine-read; the body is the rationale for human readers and never redefines token values in prose that contradicts the frontmatter.

---
version: alpha
name: Project name
description: One-line tagline
colors:
  primary: "#1A1C1E"
  secondary: "#6C7278"
  accent: "#B8422E"
  background: "#FFFFFF"
  foreground: "#1A1C1E"
typography:
  h1:
    fontFamily: "Public Sans"
    fontSize: "48px"
    fontWeight: 600
    lineHeight: 1.1
    letterSpacing: "-0.02em"
rounded:
  sm: "4px"
  md: "8px"
  lg: "16px"
spacing:
  xs: "4px"
  sm: "8px"
  md: "16px"
  lg: "32px"
components:
  button-primary:
    backgroundColor: "{colors.primary}"
    textColor: "#FFFFFF"
    rounded: "{rounded.sm}"
    padding: "12px 24px"
---

items: version is required. Colors are written as sRGB hex (#RGB, #RGBA, #RRGGBB, #RRGGBBAA). Token references use the {path.to.token} form.

Color role names are lowercase for core roles (primary, secondary, accent, background, foreground, card, muted, border, ring, destructive); text-on-background colors use onX (onPrimary) or xForeground (mutedForeground). Stay consistent within a file.
Component sub-tokens are limited to: backgroundColor, textColor, typography, rounded, padding, size, height, width.
Fonts must include the Vietnamese character set.

head: Section (exact name, exact order)
Content
rows: A north star (one metaphor) and 2 to 3 sentences on personality, density and aesthetic philosophy, ending with Key Characteristics. Includes the Register and the must-never-look-like items from PRODUCT.md
One sentence describing the palette, then each role: color name (#HEX), where it's used and why. Named Rules optional
Display and Body fonts (with fallbacks), 1 to 2 sentences on the pair's personality, then the hierarchy: level (weight, size, line height) and purpose
Grid, columns, container width, density, breakpoints, spacing rhythm on the spacing scale
Shadows or tonal layering; if flat, say so explicitly
Corner language (per rounded), border style, geometric motifs (pill, sharp, organic)
Extension section, marked NON-SPEC EXTENSION. Motion energy and which interactions animate. Short
Buttons, cards or containers, inputs. Only components that actually exist
Do: specific instructions with exact values. Don't: specific bans, with every must-never-look-like item from PRODUCT.md appearing verbatim

items: Decisive voice: 'never', 'always', 'forbidden', no 'consider' or 'may'.
Describe by feel rather than jargon: 'gently rounded corners (8px)' beats 'rounded-lg'.
No sections beyond the 9, no renaming, no made-up components.

ChatCode is an OzinTech app that connects the AI assistant you already use to software projects on your computer. tool-zalo-multi-accounts.note: An app that opens multiple Zalo accounts at once on one computer (macOS and Windows), each account in its own window, without logging out or rescanning the QR code.

sections.t: Unofficial, not affiliated with Zalo or VNG. The app renames the folders holding your Zalo messages, photos and files: back up your Zalo data before using it. Use at your own risk; the author isn't responsible for data loss.
What it is

Zalo Switcher (MIT license, README in Vietnamese) lets you keep several Zalo accounts on the same computer and open them at the same time, each with its own data folder and its own Zalo window. Good for people managing several accounts (personal, work, fanpage…) who don't want to keep logging out.
Main features

items: Each account gets its own data folder; open, switch to or close each account, or “Open all / Close all”.
Set one account as the main Zalo (renames folders, no data copying).
Back up to an external drive and restore as a new account; rename; move closed accounts to the trash.
Low disk space warning (5 GB by default), launch at login, light/dark theme, demo mode (--demo) with fake accounts to get familiar.
Includes a zalo-profiles command-line tool (status, add, open, close, main, backup, restore).

sections.t: Quick install

items.d: Download Zalo-Switcher-…-macOS.zip from Releases and drag it into Applications. Since the app isn't notarized by Apple, the first time you need to allow it in System Settings > Privacy & Security (Open Anyway).

Run ZaloSwitcher-Setup-<version>.exe (no admin rights needed) or unzip and run ZaloSwitcher.exe. SmartScreen may warn you because the file isn't signed: choose More info > Run anyway if you trust the source.
Save the Zalo account you're logged into as the main Zalo (if you aren't logged in, the first account you add becomes the main one).
Click Add account, name it, log into Zalo in the new window, then use Open on each account.

sections.t: Limits to know

items: Zalo still allows only one session per type (phone, desktop, web) per account; this tool doesn't change that rule.
Only open accounts receive messages and notifications.
Voice and video calls only work reliably in one window at a time.
Each window uses as much RAM as a separate Zalo, and each account takes a few GB of disk space.
It depends on how Zalo stores data, so a Zalo update can break the tool: read the README before updating Zalo.

What it is

zca-js is a JavaScript/TypeScript library (installed via npm or Bun, MIT license) that lets your program log into a personal Zalo account, then listen for and send messages, just like using Zalo Web. Good for personal bots, automated notifications or plugging Zalo into your workflows.

tool-phone-laptop-devmode.title: Connect your phone to a laptop with Developer Mode (Android + iOS)
tool-phone-laptop-devmode.note: Turn on Developer options, install adb, connect by cable and wirelessly, control the screen with scrcpy; iPhone: Developer Mode, Xcode, Safari Web Inspector, libimobiledevice. All commands included.

sections.t: Android can do almost everything through adb (install apps, copy files, view the screen, run commands). Apple locks the iPhone down much more: mostly logs, screen recording/mirroring and web debugging. This guide covers each system separately.
Only turn on Developer Mode / USB debugging on your own phone and only trust your own laptop. This permission gives the laptop deep control over the phone; don't use public computers.
PART 1 · ANDROID
Step 1: Turn on Developer options

items.d: Samsung: About phone → Software information. Some phones: Settings → About phone.
The phone shows “You are now a developer”. Enter your PIN/password if asked.
Usually under Settings → System → Developer options (Samsung: at the bottom of the main Settings page).
Xiaomi/Redmi: also turn on “Install via USB” and “USB debugging (Security settings)” if you want to control it with a mouse.

sections.t: Step 2: Install adb on the laptop
adb comes with Google's SDK Platform-Tools, free.

# Windows: download the zip at developer.android.com/tools/releases/platform-tools, unzip it,
# open PowerShell in that folder and type  .\adb version

# macOS
brew install --cask android-platform-tools

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install adb

# Check
adb version
Step 3: Plug in the cable and allow access

items.t: Use a USB cable that transfers data
items.d: A charge-only cable won't be detected. If the phone asks for a USB mode, choose “File transfer”.

items.t: Tap “Allow USB debugging” on the phone
items.d: Tick “Always allow from this computer” and tap Allow.
Type adb devices. A status of device means it worked.

sections.t: adb devices -l

items: unauthorized: you haven't tapped Allow on the phone. Unplug and replug the cable, or run adb kill-server then adb devices.
Device not found: try another cable/port and check that USB debugging is on. Windows may need the manufacturer's USB driver (Samsung, Xiaomi…).
Linux says “no permissions”: set up a udev rule for your phone brand, or rerun adb with the right permissions.

sections.t: Step 4: Common adb commands

# Install / uninstall apps
adb install app.apk
adb install -r app.apk          # reinstall, keep data
adb uninstall com.ten.goi

# Copy files
adb push file.txt /sdcard/Download/
adb pull /sdcard/DCIM/Camera/ ./anh

# Take a screenshot
adb shell screencap -p /sdcard/s.png
adb pull /sdcard/s.png

# Record the screen (max 3 minutes by default, Ctrl+C to stop)
adb shell screenrecord /sdcard/demo.mp4
adb pull /sdcard/demo.mp4

# Open a shell on the phone / view logs
adb shell
adb logcat

# List installed apps
adb shell pm list packages

# Type and tap remotely
adb shell input text hello
adb shell input tap 540 1200
adb shell input keyevent 4      # 4=Back, 3=Home, 26=Power

# Reboot
adb reboot

# When adb hangs
adb kill-server
adb start-server
Step 5: Connect wirelessly (Android 11 and later)
The phone and laptop must be on the same Wi-Fi network. You only need to pair once per laptop.

items.d: Developer options → Wireless debugging → on.
Tap “Pair device with pairing code”. The phone shows a pairing IP:port and a 6-digit code.

items.t: Run the pair command on the laptop
items.d: Type adb pair IP:PAIRING-PORT and enter the 6-digit code.
The main Wireless debugging screen shows a different IP:port (the connection port). Type adb connect IP:CONNECT-PORT. This port may change each time you turn it back on.

sections.t:
adb pair 192.168.1.20:37099
# enter the 6-digit code when asked
adb connect 192.168.1.20:41555
adb devices

# Disconnect
adb disconnect
sections.cap: Example (replace with the IP and ports on your phone)

sections.t: Android 10 and earlier: plug in the cable once, type adb tcpip 5555, unplug, then adb connect phone-IP:5555.
Step 6: View and control the phone screen on the laptop (scrcpy)
scrcpy is an open-source tool. It needs no app on the phone and uses the same adb connection above (cable or wireless). You can control the phone with your mouse and keyboard.

# Windows (if you have winget) or download the zip from the GitHub page (adb included)
winget install --exact Genymobile.scrcpy

# macOS
brew install scrcpy

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install scrcpy

# Run (phone has USB debugging on and is connected)
scrcpy

# Common options
scrcpy --turn-screen-off --stay-awake     # turn off the phone screen, keep it awake
scrcpy --max-size 1024                    # lower the resolution for smoother playback
scrcpy --record demo.mp4                  # watch and record at the same time
scrcpy -s SERIAL                          # pick a device when several are connected
Install commands and option names may differ depending on your scrcpy version and OS. Check the scrcpy README on GitHub for the latest commands.
Turn it off when not in use

items: Turn off USB debugging and Wireless debugging when you're done.
Developer options → “Revoke USB debugging authorizations” to remove trusted laptops.

sections.t: PART 2 · iPHONE (iOS)

Know this first: iPhone has no adb. Apple doesn't let a laptop control the screen remotely like Android. What you can do: view logs, record/mirror the screen, debug web pages in Safari, install dev apps with Xcode (Mac).
Step 1: Trust the computer

items.t: Plug the iPhone into the laptop with a cable
items.d: Use a Lightning/USB-C cable that transfers data.
Enter your passcode when asked. On Windows, also install the Apple Devices app (or iTunes) for the driver, otherwise the phone won't be detected.

sections.t: Step 2: Turn on Developer Mode (iOS 16 and later)

items.d: Scroll to the bottom and find “Developer Mode”.
The iPhone will ask to restart.
Unlock the phone, tap “Turn On” and enter your passcode.

sections.t: The Developer Mode option may not appear until the iPhone has been connected to Xcode on a Mac or has a dev build of an app installed. This is how iOS works, not a problem with your phone.
Step 3A: If you have a Mac

items.d: Open Xcode → Window → Devices and Simulators. Tick “Connect via network” to connect wirelessly after pairing by cable.
Open QuickTime Player → File → New Movie Recording, click the arrow next to the record button and choose the iPhone as the source.

iPhone: Settings → Safari → Advanced → turn on Web Inspector (on newer iOS it may be under Settings → Apps → Safari). Mac: Safari → Settings → Advanced → turn on “Show features for web developers”. Open the page on the iPhone, then go to the Develop menu on the Mac and choose the iPhone's name and the page to inspect.

sections.t: Step 3B: If you use Windows or Linux
The open-source libimobiledevice toolkit can read device info and logs. Some commands (like screenshots) depend on the iOS version: iOS 17 and later need a different tool, e.g. pymobiledevice3.

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install libimobiledevice

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install libimobiledevice-utils usbmuxd

# Pair and check
idevicepair pair
idevice_id -l                 # list UDIDs
ideviceinfo                   # device info
idevicesyslog                 # live logs
idevicescreenshot shot.png    # may not work on iOS 17+

# iOS 17+: pymobiledevice3 (requires Python)
pip install pymobiledevice3
pymobiledevice3 usbmux list
pymobiledevice3 syslog live
Some pymobiledevice3 commands on iOS 17+ need a “tunnel” running and admin rights. See the project's docs on GitHub for the syntax for your version.
Mirror the iPhone screen to a laptop without a cable

items: Mac: use Control Center on the iPhone → Screen Mirroring, or QuickTime with a cable as above.
Windows: Windows can't receive AirPlay out of the box. You need a third-party AirPlay receiver app. Check its reliability and price yourself before using it.
This guide hasn't tested each third-party app individually.

sections.t: Important notes before use

items: Facebook's terms restrict automated access. Only use it on your own account, at a human-like pace, and accept the risk of account restrictions. This is the repo README's own assessment.
Login cookies live in the ~/.cache/fb profile (or %LOCALAPPDATA%\fb on Windows). Anyone who can read this folder can use your session, so treat it like a password.
The headless Chrome is controlled via the DevTools protocol on a random 127.0.0.1 port with no authentication. Only use it on a personal machine, not a shared one.
Post, comment, send and delete commands are real actions on your account. With an AI agent, try read-only mode first and require confirmation before posting or sending.
Facebook's interface can change at any time, so the tool may need updates. The repo states clearly that not every feature is guaranteed to be tested.
End-to-end encrypted chats need your Messenger PIN: pass it via the FB_PIN variable or stdin, not as a command argument.

tool-cloakbrowser.title: CloakBrowser: a Chromium drop-in for Playwright with C++-level fingerprint patches
tool-cloakbrowser.note: A custom Chromium build that drops straight into Playwright, 87 C++-level patches, with humanize and proxy support. Wrapper code is MIT, the binary needs a license key.

sections.t: Use responsibly: this is a browser that spoofs device identity for automation. Only use it on your own sites, on public data you're allowed to collect, or with permission. Automation that breaks terms of service (especially on Facebook, Zalo, TikTok...) can get accounts banned and may be illegal. CloakBrowser's README also explicitly forbids unauthorized automation, credential stuffing and abusive account creation.

Info taken from the repo's GitHub page, read on 4/11/2026. Stars, versions and terms may have changed, and the claims about passing bot checks come from the author; I haven't verified them independently.
Quick comparison with Camoufox

head: Criteria
CloakBrowser
Camoufox
rows: MIT wrapper, binary needs a license key
Free tier limited to one concurrent session, Pro plan available
Linux, Windows, macOS, doesn't run on WSL
Under development, may not be stable for production

sections.t: My take: if you need Chromium, want a supported prebuilt binary and are fine with a license key, look at CloakBrowser. If you need fully open source with no key, and can accept the Firefox engine and the 'not stable for production' note, look at Camoufox. Either way, test it on your own use case.
Repo info

head: Item
Details
rows: A custom Chromium build, a drop-in replacement for Playwright (Puppeteer supported)
Linux x86_64 and arm64, macOS arm64 and x86_64, Windows x86_64
About 32.7k stars, 2.7k forks, 137 open issues, 390 commits
Wrapper code (Python, JS, .NET): MIT. Chromium binary: separate license, needs a license key
README says 'Last tested: Nov 2026' and describes itself as maintained

sections.t: Highlights

items: Fingerprints are patched in Chromium's C++ source, not via JavaScript injection or config flags. The binary's Ed25519 signature is verified before extraction.
humanize=True: Bézier-curve mouse movement, typing with random delays, natural-paced scrolling.
HTTP and SOCKS5 proxy support, geoip=True to match timezone and language to the proxy IP, WebRTC IP spoofing.
Persistent profiles (keeps cookies and localStorage between runs) and Chrome extension loading.
Poses as Windows by default on Linux and Windows, with an optional macOS identity.
cloakserve runs the browser as a CDP server; there's a Docker image, a .NET client and a CLI (install binary, diagnostics, cache management).

sections.t: Installation

pip install cloakbrowser

npm install cloakbrowser playwright-core   # or puppeteer-core

dotnet add package CloakBrowser

items: The ~200 MB binary downloads automatically on first run and is cached. No need to run playwright install chromium, but you still need the system libraries Playwright requires.
launch() returns a Playwright Browser object, so new_page(), close()... work as usual. Switching from Playwright only means changing the browser launch code.

sections.t: License and license key (important)

head: Plan
Terms
rows: Sign up with email to get a key, one concurrent session. Always gets the latest build
More concurrent sessions, can pin a Chromium version to roll back
Personal and commercial per the README, no redistributing the binary. Serving third parties needs an OEM or SaaS license

items: Every launch needs the key, set via the CLOAKBROWSER_LICENSE_KEY environment variable. Don't put the key in source code or chats.
The keyless v146 binary is only in the old wrapper (pip install "cloakbrowser<0.7") and no longer gets updates.
Full terms are in the repo's BINARY-LICENSE.md; read it before commercial use.

sections.t: Limitations the README admits

items: It doesn't solve CAPTCHAs, it tries to keep them from appearing. No built-in proxy rotation; you bring your own proxies.
Some sites still detect headless mode; running headed is recommended (use Xvfb on Linux).
On Linux, a convincing Windows identity needs real Windows fonts installed, and a macOS identity needs real Mac fonts.
Puppeteer can be detected by reCAPTCHA Enterprise, so Playwright is recommended. page.wait_for_timeout() and page.evaluate() may send CDP commands some systems can spot.
Playwright's context.request and route.fetch() don't go through SOCKS5 or authenticated proxies.
The README admits detection may catch up in the future; it's an ongoing arms race.

sections.t: Ideas for using it in the Library

items: Test your own website and landing pages across many browser setups and regions.
Run browser agents on a VPS (pairs with the OVH VPS for Hermes Agent guide) to get blocked by mistake less often when accessing public data you're allowed to use.
Study how anti-bot systems work, in your own environment.

sections.t: Install safety notes

items: There are many forks and look-alikes (such as zapabob, DivMode, dgtlmoon, Munasco) with different numbers. Only use the official CloakHQ/CloakBrowser repo and the author's own PyPI or npm packages.
The prebuilt binary is downloaded from the publisher, so run it in an isolated environment (a separate VPS or Docker), away from API keys, passwords or important data.

Details

items: Each launch gets a consistent device identity, generated from real-world device distributions.
Fingerprint spoofing: navigator, screen, WebGL, WebGPU, fonts, audio, voices, media devices, timezone, locale, geolocation, WebRTC IP.
humanize=True: human-like mouse movement, based on recordings of real interactions.

camoufox fetch

npm install camoufox playwright-core

with Camoufox(headless=True) as browser:
    page = browser.new_page()
    # use it like regular Playwright
The returned browser is a standard Playwright Browser. In Node.js use const browser = await Camoufox({ headless: true }).
Main options

head: Option
What it does
rows: True, or the max seconds per mouse movement
proxy with geoip=True so timezone, language, location and WebRTC IP match the exit IP
True, or 'virtual' and 'virtual-gpu' (the last two on Linux only)

fingerprint_preset, locale, addons, exclude_addons, pin_cpu_cores, main_world_eval, launch_server()

Operating systems

items: Builds run on Linux; Windows and macOS versions are cross-compiled. Packaged architectures: x86_64, arm64, and i686 (Windows only).

items: Camoufox only spoofs Firefox identities. Some systems check SpiderMonkey-specific behavior, so it can't pass as Chromium.
Canvas on an OS different from the real machine returns random data and can give it away. Audio rendering and text width results aren't noised.
Enabling instantAnimations can get the browser detected. Media codecs on Linux depend on the libraries installed on the machine.
The README admits Camoufox can still be detected.

sections.t: I couldn't open DJI's download page (the domain was blocked), so I haven't seen the file name, version or instructions there. What follows is based on the page title (D-Log M to Rec.709 for Osmo Pocket 3) and articles I found on the web. The specific steps come from secondary sources, so compare them with DJI's page.
What this download is for

Osmo Pocket 3 can shoot in D-Log M mode: a flat, washed-out image that keeps more highlight and shadow detail for grading. That footage needs converting to a normal color standard to view. The file on DJI's page is a LUT that converts D-Log M to Rec.709, the color space for regular screens. Going by the page title, it's a file for the editing stage, after shooting.
Where it sits in the Edit library
It's in the Editing group because the file is used in editing software. It assumes you shot in D-Log M. If you shot in a normal color mode, you don't need this LUT.
How to use it (from secondary sources, not checked on DJI's page)

head: Software

rows: Per DJI's LUT guide (a 2018 version written for Resolve 15 and older cameras): copy the file into Color Management's LUT folder, in a DJI subfolder, then click Update Lists (only needed once). From a third-party tutorial: load the LUT in Lumetri Color, under Basic Correction, Input LUT, then fine-tune with curves and color wheels. This is a secondary source; the menu path isn't confirmed

One article notes Premiere Pro sometimes has issues with DJI files, so test a short clip before editing the whole project.

A 2h03 lecture video on a Windows laptop with the whisper small model: slide detection took about 3 min 22 s, transcription about 51 minutes, and it produced 88 slides and notes with 8 parts and 19 sections. items: Python 3.9 or later, and ffmpeg

Things to know

items: The speech and slide images are sent to the Anthropic API when you use the Claude step. Do not use videos with personal or internal information unless you have permission.
Automatic transcription can get terms wrong. What Claude is unsure about is marked “Needs checking”. You still need to read it through before using it.
Claude only uses the speech and the text on the slides and adds no outside knowledge. If something drifts from what the lecturer meant, compare it with the original speech section in recap.html.
Notion does not keep key-takeaway boxes and columns when importing Markdown; the boxes become plain quote blocks.
Only use videos you have the right to use.

You can stop midway with Ctrl+C and rerun the exact same command: the tool saves the part of the video already downloaded, slide detection, transcription (every 30 seconds) and the Claude step results, so it only does the rest.

tool-drive-ebook-reader.title: Drive Ebook Reader: read large PDF/EPUB files on Google Drive without downloading
tool-drive-ebook-reader.note: A Chrome/Edge extension that fetches only the part you are reading through the Drive API, so multi-hundred-MB files open at once even when Drive cannot preview them. Pick your books once in the Drive window; data flows straight from Google to your browser, through no server.

sections.t: Drive often says "preview unavailable" for thick PDFs and cannot open EPUB at all, forcing you to download the whole file. This extension opens the book right in a browser tab: the PDF is requested in 1 MB pieces exactly where you are reading, so not a single byte lands on your disk.
What it does

head: Type
What the extension does
rows: Fetched in chunks over HTTP Range, lazy page rendering, zoom, fit width, text selection and copy, remembers your page
Table of contents, page turns, font size, remembers position; loaded in memory, never written to disk
Exported to PDF through the Drive API, then read
Picked books are remembered on your device; select several at once in the Drive window
Opens PDF/EPUB from your computer; PDFs are read in slices too

sections.t: Install

items.d: Download the ZIP with the button below and unzip it into a permanent folder (for example D:\lanhmar\drive-ebook-reader).
Open chrome://extensions (Edge: edge://extensions), turn on Developer mode, click Load unpacked and pick the unzipped folder. The extension ID is always bijcnaofiojlemmbghgcljfekdaoghbf.

Click the extension icon → “Pick books from Google Drive”, sign in and select one or more books in the Drive window. They land in your Library and open at once; next time the purple “Read without downloading” button on that book's Drive page opens it directly.

sections.t: How access works: the extension only requests Google's drive.file scope, so it can read exactly the books you pick in the Google Drive window and nothing else. Click “Pick books from Google Drive” once (several at a time is fine); they go into your Library and open directly from then on, including from the purple button on the Drive page. No test-user list, no download to disk.
How it works

items: Signs in with chrome.identity using the drive.file scope: Google grants access only to the files you pick in the Google Picker (hosted at lanhmar.id.vn/drive-picker.html), nothing else; the extension only talks to www.googleapis.com.
PDF.js gets a custom PDFDataRangeTransport: whenever it needs data it sends a Range header to the Drive API and receives 206 Partial Content, 1 MB at a time, with background auto-fetch turned off.
Only pages near the viewport are rendered and far pages are released to save RAM; the top bar shows exactly how much data has been fetched.
Tested with a 24 MB PDF: opening fetched about 3 MB, jumping to page 20 another 4 MB. PDFs whose page dictionaries are scattered through the file may need most of the file on first open.
Reading position, font size and the light/sepia/dark theme are stored in chrome.storage.local on your machine.
